newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia PM likely to turn to right for new govt.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia PM likely to turn to right for new govt.

text.p: Slovenia's centre-left Liberal Democrats, biggest winners in a general election, faced an uphill task in seeking coalition partners with first offers likely to go to the right, political analysts said on Monday.
The Liberal Democrats led by Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek won 27.1 percent of votes in Sunday's general election, the second since Slovenian independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.

Most analysts and political commentators said President Milan Kucan was almost certain to call on Drnovsek to form the next government, but final unofficial results showed that the prime minister may have to steer a delicate course.
"The poor new Prime Minister," the leftwing daily Republika said. "The government will be pretty hard to form."

The Liberal Democrats were pitted against an informal alliance of rightist parties, called the "Slovenian Spring", which together may clinch a majority in the 90-seat parliament once the complex proportional representation calculations of the vote are finalised.
The alliance included the rightwing People's Party, which won 19.59 percent, the centre-right Social Democrats with 16.03 percent and the Christian Democrats who took 9.52 percent.
Final official results were expected to be issued by the National Electoral Commission by the end of the week.
"Drnovsek will most likely be called to form a new government but he will have to negotiate hard," Drago Zajc, politics professor at Ljubljana University, told Reuters.
"The new coalition will probably include Liberal Democrats, the People's Party and Christian Democrats," he said.
Respected newspaper Delo took the same line, saying the three party coalition was Drnovsek's best-case scenario.

But Slovenian political analyst Miha Kovac said it was not yet plain sailing for Drnovsek with the final shareout of seats very tight. Postal votes, which usually favour the right, still had to be counted.
"At the moment I calculate that the 'Spring' parties have 45 seats and if postal votes give them another seat, they will try to form the next coalition government," Kovac told Reuters.
A clear shift to the right, without the Liberal Democrats in government, could spell trouble for Slovenia, he said.
Drnovsek has been the loudest advocate of membership of NATO and the European Union and of pushing harder to liberalise the Slovenian economy.
Slovenia's rightwing parties prefer a more cautious approach to foreign investment, near-hostility to foreign ownership of property and coolness towards EU membership.

Marjan Podobnik, whose People's Party won most votes among the parties of the "Slovenian Spring", is at best lukewarm over EU membership and has demanded a long transition period and wants to protect the jobs of farmers, who back his party.
Kovac said a rightist government would slow down the already sluggish privatisation process and may want to revise privatisations which have taken place over the past four years.
"If they form a government, foreign investment will stay in the doldrums. The climate will be more favourable if Drnovsek stays in power," he added.
Slovenia's stock exchange viewed the uncertainty with pessimism. Trading in shares was expected to remain sluggish until a new government was formed, banking analyst Toni Apollonio said.
